headline: Edge0 reports SSD-streamed MoE inference with trained one-token-ahead routing
dek: AutoArk’s Edge0 paper reports serving its int4 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory at 20.4 tokens/s decode and 2.9 GiB peak active memory, using SSD-streamed experts and a trained prerouter that predicts one token ahead. In a same-session MacBook M2 16 GB comparison where the 18.4 GiB checkpoint does not fit, the paper reports 6.4 versus 3.5 tokens/s at routing width K=4 against on-demand streaming. These are author-reported measurements from one implementation and hardware family. The paper reports a 3.9-point mean gap to the fp16 base across five benchmarks, with a 6.1-point AIME gap; concurrency, other storage tiers, independent reproduction and broader deployment are unestablished.
what_changed: AutoArk’s Edge0 paper reports serving its int4 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory at 20.4 tokens/s decode and 2.9 GiB peak active memory, using SSD-streamed experts and a trained prerouter that predicts one token ahead. In a same-session MacBook M2 16 GB comparison where the 18.4 GiB checkpoint does not fit, the paper reports 6.4 versus 3.5 tokens/s at routing width K=4 against on-demand streaming. These are author-reported measurements from one implementation and hardware family. The paper reports a 3.9-point mean gap to the fp16 base across five benchmarks, with a 6.1-point AIME gap; concurrency, other storage tiers, independent reproduction and broader deployment are unestablished.
why_it_matters: The work combines static-weight SSD placement with predicted expert routing to target the weight-memory limit of local sparse-MoE inference. If reproduced, its measured memory and decode profile could expand the models that fit on consumer hardware. Its value depends on storage latency, cache residency, model quality, and single-request workloads; the paper does not establish general cross-platform performance.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB unified memory, the authors report 20.4 tokens/s decode and 2.9 GiB peak active memory for the 35B tier.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a same-session, three-round median comparison on a 16 GB MacBook M2 with an 18.4 GiB checkpoint, the authors report K=4 prerouter decode at 6.4 tokens/s versus 3.5 for on-demand streaming.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five OpenCompass benchmarks, the authors report a 3.9-point mean score gap between the 35B int4 Edge0 pipeline and its fp16 base, including a 6.1-point AIME gap.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The public repository README lists engines for macOS, iOS, Android and Windows, while its Python MLX framework is currently limited to Apple Silicon; the paper’s measured implementation is MLX.

technical.claimed_result: The authors claim SSD streaming plus one-token-ahead predicted routing hides expert-load latency while keeping peak active memory near the working set; their reported 35B Apple Silicon profile is 20.4 tokens/s at 2.9 GiB.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports a 24 GB Mac mini M4 Pro for its release profile and a 16 GB MacBook M2 for paired prerouter A/B. It provides no cloud-price, energy or total-cost comparison.
technical.demonstrated_result: Authors report 20.4 tokens/s decode, 2.9 GiB peak active memory and 113/140 tokens/s cold/warm prefill for the 35B tier on the Mac mini M4 Pro. For K=4 on the 16 GB MacBook M2, paired three-round medians are 6.4 tokens/s prerouter versus 3.5 on-demand. They report 79.2 average versus 83.2 for fp16 across five benchmarks, with AIME 86.6 vs 92.7. Author-reported; no independent verification.
technical.implementation_status: The linked public repository contains a Python/MLX implementation and separate platform-native engines; repository support statements do not establish their measured performance. the research desk inspected README only and did not install or run the code.
technical.mechanism: Move static expert weights to SSD, stage predicted next-token expert sets during current-token compute, and train the routing replacement and recovery LoRA together.
technical.novelty: Combines SSD expert offload with a trained cross-token prerouter whose selected experts define the actual route, and an unmerged recovery adapter trained on the deployed student path.
technical.regime: Paper measurements use a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB for the release profile and a MacBook M2 with 16 GB for same-session paired A/B prerouter tests. The measured 35B tier is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at int4, K=4, 40 layers and 256 experts. Quality comparison is against the fp16 base over five OpenCompass benchmarks. One request at a time.
technical.reproducibility: The paper supplies detailed paired protocols, tables, implementation claims and a public repository; the research desk did not independently run the implementation. The repository README gives a distinct two-run speed range that should remain separate from the paper’s paired 20.4 tokens/s result. A separate user issue reports garbled output on Apple A18 Pro / MacBook Neo; the closed issue has no visible maintainer diagnosis or resolution. A second closed user issue reports 0.66–0.81 tokens/s on an 8 GB M1 and hypothesizes a small-mmap-read/page-fault bottleneck; that causal account is unverified, with no visible maintainer response.
technical.strongest_baseline: Same-session on-demand streaming at matched cache budget for prerouter speed comparisons; original fp16 base under identical OpenCompass settings for quality. The fully resident baseline is also reported on the same Mac mini but is memory constrained.

limitations: All performance and benchmark comparisons are author-reported; no independent execution was conducted.

The main reported device is a Mac mini M4 Pro; the prerouter comparison is a MacBook M2 with 16 GB unified memory and an 18.4 GiB checkpoint that does not fit. Results are hardware, cache and protocol specific.
The paper reports single-request FIFO serving; batching and concurrency are untested.
The paper identifies graph-building/CPU work as a decode floor and says benefits shrink on hot caches or fast storage.
The 35B tier trails its fp16 base by 6.1 points on AIME 2026; the 8B tier trails by 10 points.
The repository lists platform engines beyond macOS, but the paper’s measured implementation is MLX on Apple Silicon; cross-platform performance is not demonstrated.

An individual GitHub issue reports garbled outputs on Apple A18 Pro / MacBook Neo with pinned MLX versions and crashes after an MLX upgrade. The issue is closed without a visible maintainer resolution; it is an unverified compatibility report, not an independent benchmark reproduction.

A separate closed user issue reports 0.66–0.81 tokens/s for the 8B model on an 8 GB Apple M1, far below the README’s M4 Pro range; it includes same-session controls but has no visible maintainer response. It is an unverified single-device report and does not contradict the M4 Pro result directly.
contradictory_evidence: Quality is not uniform: the paper reports the 35B Edge0 score at 86.6 versus 92.7 for fp16 on AIME 2026, a 6.1-point deficit. It also reports page-cache displacement and increased unreclaimable residency with prerouting; on fast storage or hot caches the gains shrink.

The repository README’s two-run benchmark lists 14.9–17.7 tokens/s for the 35B model, while the paper’s paired short-context table reports 20.4 tokens/s; these are different benchmark protocols and should not be conflated.

A user report in Edge0 issue #8 describes incoherent output from both model tiers on a MacBook Neo with Apple A18 Pro using the README-pinned MLX versions; the report also says later MLX versions crashed. The issue page is closed but shows no maintainer diagnosis or resolution. This single unverified report concerns a different device and does not test the paper’s Mac mini M4 Pro measurements.

A second user report in Edge0 issue #17 reports 0.66–0.81 tokens/s for edge0-8b on an 8 GB Apple M1 MacBook Pro, versus about 23–25 tokens/s in the model card; it gives repeat timings, environment details and an 11.38 tokens/s same-session dense-model control, and hypothesizes small mmap-read/page-fault costs on the M1. The issue page is closed with no visible maintainer response. This is one unverified report on a different device; the causal explanation is the user’s hypothesis.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent execution or reproduction of the paper’s speed, active-memory or quality measurements was conducted. The paper reports single-device Apple Silicon results; a 16 GB comparison has high cross-session variability. Two separate user issues report garbled output on Apple A18 Pro and much lower speed on an 8 GB M1; neither has visible maintainer resolution.
The paper evaluates one request at a time and identifies concurrency, storage-tier transfer and larger batch working sets as untested; non-MLX code paths are not evaluated in its paper benchmarks.

headline: A 157-project audit reports fragmented QA coverage across open-source AI agents
dek: Dai et al. report a repository-level audit of 157 popular open-source LLM-agent projects, selected from public GitHub projects with at least 100 stars as of May 2026. They coded documentation, source, configuration, tests and structured evidence across execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts and risk scenarios. Their coding identifies recurring gaps, including inconsistent controls across overlapping action paths (152/157 projects, 96.8%) and sparse boundary, adversarial and multi-step tool-use testing. These are author-reported descriptions of inspectable repository artifacts; the study does not measure deployed failure rates, establish that a listed risk is an exploitable vulnerability, or show that safeguards are effective at runtime.

Their coding identifies recurring gaps, including inconsistent controls across overlapping action paths (152/157 projects, 96.8%) and sparse boundary, adversarial and multi-step tool-use testing. These are author-reported descriptions of inspectable repository artifacts; the study does not measure deployed failure rates, establish that a listed risk is an exploitable vulnerability, or show that safeguards are effective at runtime.
why_it_matters: If the audit’s coding generalizes, checking an agent’s individual tools is insufficient: assurance also needs to trace whether authorization, containment and tests cover equivalent paths through tools, plugins, browsers, filesystems and external APIs. The study gives evaluators a concrete repository-level framework, while its popularity-filtered sample and descriptive method limit prevalence claims.

headline: PreDE reports a policy-specific gate for screening robot-policy quantization before closed-loop tests
dek: Xu et al. introduce PreDE, which calibrates policy-specific thresholds from a small set of quantized configurations with known closed-loop outcomes, then uses action deviation on a fixed observation log to accept, reject or defer new candidates. In the paper, 21 of 28 held-out configurations across Cosmos Policy and UVA received decisions, all matching their observed labels; seven were deferred, including both acceptable and degraded outcomes. A separate 450-trial Franka Research 3 study reports significant degradation for configurations assigned to high-deviation groups before trials, while low-deviation results were not statistically significant. W4A4 reduced median action-query latency 1.37× and peak memory about 44% on the tested setup. These are author-reported results, conditional on each policy and evaluation setting.
what_changed: Xu et al. introduce PreDE, which calibrates policy-specific thresholds from a small set of quantized configurations with known closed-loop outcomes, then uses action deviation on a fixed observation log to accept, reject or defer new candidates. In the paper, 21 of 28 held-out configurations across Cosmos Policy and UVA received decisions, all matching their observed labels; seven were deferred, including both acceptable and degraded outcomes. A separate 450-trial Franka Research 3 study reports significant degradation for configurations assigned to high-deviation groups before trials, while low-deviation results were not statistically significant. W4A4 reduced median action-query latency 1.37× and peak memory about 44% on the tested setup. These are author-reported results, conditional on each policy and evaluation setting.
why_it_matters: Robot-policy quantization can save memory and latency, but nominal bit width does not predict task loss consistently. A calibrated offline screen could help prioritize expensive closed-loop evaluations, provided its abstentions, policy-specific scope and finite-trial uncertainty remain visible.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that PreDE issued decisions for 21 of 28 held-out configurations across two policies (75% coverage), and all issued decisions matched the observed acceptable or degraded labels; seven candidates were deferred.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a separate 450-trial Franka Research 3 study, the authors report significant degradation for every tested high-deviation configuration selected before trials; low-deviation comparisons did not reach significance, which does not establish equivalence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the reported RTX 5080 setup, W4A4 reduced median action-query latency by 1.37× and peak allocated memory by about 44% relative to bf16.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: PreDE’s thresholds are policy- and setting-specific, and its accept/reject interpretation is conditional on a within-setting ordering hypothesis; uncertain cases require closed-loop evidence.

technical.claimed_result: The authors argue that policy-specific behavioral calibration can screen some quantization configurations offline and defer uncertain cases for closed-loop evaluation. They report that nominal bit width alone and a shared deviation threshold fail to explain task outcomes across the tested policies/settings.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports 450 robot task trials plus a separate 45-episode resource-measurement collection. On an RTX 5080, W4A4 action-query median latency was 1485 ms versus 2030 ms for bf16; peak allocated memory was 2.93 GB versus 5.19 GB. Full development/calibration costs and total robot-time economics are not reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The authors report that across 28 held-out Cosmos Policy and UVA configurations, the rule issued 21 decisions (75% coverage), all matching observed acceptable/degraded labels; seven were deferred, comprising three acceptable, one degraded and three unresolved outcomes. In a separate Franka Research 3 study, deviation groups were fixed before 450 trials across two independently fine-tuned Cosmos policies; all tested high-deviation configurations had significant degradation, while low-deviation comparisons did not reach significance and do not establish equivalence. On the RTX 5080 setup, W4A4 reduced median action-query latency from 2030 to 1485 ms (1.37×) and peak allocated memory from 5.19 to 2.93 GB (about 44%). These are paper-reported results.
technical.implementation_status: Authors provide a public Apache-2.0 GitHub repository with Python package, adapters, examples and tests. The repository landing page and README were inspected; the research desk did not execute the code or reproduce the results.
technical.mechanism: PreDE replays a fixed log of observations through a reference and quantized policy and measures action deviation. It calibrates two thresholds using quantized configurations with known closed-loop labels for a fixed policy, task distribution, control protocol and outcome rule. New configurations below the acceptance threshold are accepted, above the rejection threshold are rejected, and those between are deferred to closed-loop testing. The interpretation depends on a within-setting single-crossing label-ordering hypothesis.
technical.novelty: Calibrates offline action deviation to policy-specific closed-loop outcomes, and explicitly abstains when development evidence cannot distinguish acceptable from degraded behavior; separates quantization deviation measurement from task-performance prediction.
technical.regime: Five world action models across four benchmark settings; held-out prediction covers 20 Cosmos Policy and eight UVA configurations on LIBERO-10, with thresholds calibrated from policy-specific development outcomes. A separate physical study tests two independently fine-tuned Cosmos policies on a Franka Research 3 for cup placement and cube selection. The real-robot deviation groups are prospective but are not the same as PreDE’s calibrated threshold rule.
technical.reproducibility: The paper gives methods, thresholds, benchmark results and a public repository, but no independent reproduction was performed. Threshold validity depends on an explicit within-setting label-ordering hypothesis and recalibration when policy, task or measurement protocol changes.
technical.strongest_baseline: For prediction, the paper compares PreDE with post hoc fixed deviation and bit-width rules at 100% coverage; those rules falsely rejected six and five acceptable held-out candidates, respectively. Quantization outcomes are compared with matched bf16 references and task-specific closed-loop success.

limitations: The empirical results are author-reported; no independent execution or reproduction was performed in this review.
The held-out prediction set covers only two calibrated policies and 28 configurations; all seven deferred cases needed closed-loop evidence to settle their outcomes.
The decision rule relies on a within-setting label-ordering hypothesis; policy, task, control protocol, observation log or labeling changes may require recalibration.
The real-robot test uses two fine-tuned Cosmos policies and small task-specific trial counts; its deviation groups do not establish population-wide safety or performance preservation.
The absence of statistical significance in low-deviation comparisons does not establish equivalence or non-inferiority.
The public repository was inspected but not run; independent validation of artifacts and reported measurements remains open.

evidence_gaps.description: PreDE prediction results and repository code have not been independently executed or reproduced.
The real-robot low-deviation comparisons are too small to establish non-inferiority; PreDE’s threshold results are limited to two simulation-calibrated policies.

headline: SimLife-BP tests long-horizon behavioral-rule inference in synthetic household simulations
dek: Peng et al. present SimLife-BP, a benchmark for inferring symbolic behavioral patterns from long synthetic household timelines. The current v2 paper describes 106 episodes, up to 48.23 hours and 120 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs; tasks test direct, counterfactual, noisy-counterfactual and inverse reasoning under three hint levels. Across reported model evaluations, performance depends strongly on the evidence pipeline: most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average question accuracy, while Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with full hints over noiseless text-only evidence. The authors also report shortcutting by frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when patterns change. These are paper-reported results in scripted Sims 4 simulations with deterministic symbolic rules and generated dialogue, not evidence of real human understanding or deployed household-agent performance.
what_changed: Peng et al. present SimLife-BP, a benchmark for inferring symbolic behavioral patterns from long synthetic household timelines. The current v2 paper describes 106 episodes, up to 48.23 hours and 120 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs; tasks test direct, counterfactual, noisy-counterfactual and inverse reasoning under three hint levels. Across reported model evaluations, performance depends strongly on the evidence pipeline: most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average question accuracy, while Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with full hints over noiseless text-only evidence. The authors also report shortcutting by frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when patterns change. These are paper-reported results in scripted Sims 4 simulations with deterministic symbolic rules and generated dialogue, not evidence of real human understanding or deployed household-agent performance.
why_it_matters: The benchmark separates long-context storage from the harder task of inferring and revising a behavioral rule when evidence is distributed across time and modalities. Its large reported gap between raw video-plus-language and structured noiseless text shows that evaluation can be dominated by evidence extraction and organization before rule reasoning is measured. The synthetic deterministic rules and staged diary-summary pipeline make the result useful for evaluation design but limit claims about people or real-world assistants.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The current v2 paper describes 106 synthetic episodes up to 48.23 hours/120 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs and four reasoning question types at three hint levels.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s full-hint noiseless text-only condition, Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy; most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average accuracy.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report frequency-based shortcuts and difficulty adapting when patterns change, within scripted Sims 4 simulations; no real-human or deployed-agent transfer is established.

technical.claimed_result: The authors argue that models may predict frequent outcomes without recovering the underlying rule, and that performance improves when relevant evidence is cleaner and structured. Their v2 paper reports these patterns within its scripted, deterministic synthetic environment; external validity is unestablished.
technical.compute_or_cost: The appendix reports evaluation can take several hours to seven days per model using vLLM 0.19.0 on one to four NVIDIA A40 GPUs; total benchmark-generation and end-to-end inference costs were not reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v2 paper describes 106 episodes up to 48.23 hours/120 in-game days and 1,439 questions, organized into 381 tasks per hint level. It reports that most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average accuracy; under full hints, Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with noiseless text-only evidence (L-N). Authors report frequent reliance on simple frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when behavioral patterns change. These results are author-reported benchmark measurements.
technical.implementation_status: The authors provide a project website and describe a simulation/data-generation and evaluation pipeline. the research desk inspected the primary paper but did not execute the benchmark code or independently validate the generated episodes.
technical.mechanism: SimLife simulates multi-character household activity in The Sims 4 with visual observations, game-action logs and generated dialogue. SimLife-BP builds long video chains from days whose actions satisfy explicit temporal or event-based if-then rules, then asks four binary question types—direct prediction, counterfactual, noisy counterfactual and inverse reasoning—at three rule-hint levels. The visual baseline first summarizes video windows into diaries and then answers from concatenated text; text-only baselines receive cleaner structured inputs.
technical.novelty: Combines extended simulated household timelines, multimodal contextual cues, explicit underlying behavioral rules, four complementary reasoning queries and dynamic pattern changes in a benchmark designed to distinguish surface prediction from rule inference.
technical.regime: Synthetic household activity built on The Sims 4. Episodes use scripted deterministic symbolic rules with temporal or event-based conditions; video and generated dialogue are aligned with simulator action logs. Tasks contain four binary question types and three hint levels. The vision pipeline summarizes windows before text-only QA; the noiseless language-only condition provides structured oracle-filtered evidence.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes episode construction, rule formalization, question design and input pipelines. The public artifacts and model runs have not been independently executed; simulation and generated-dialogue validity and transfer to independently collected human behavior remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the paper, modality and evidence-pipeline comparisons include vision-plus-language diary summaries, language-only responses over noisier action-log text (L), and language-only responses over noiseless structured text (L-N), with full, partial and no-hint conditions. The comparison reveals input/evidence effects but does not isolate a general reasoning mechanism independent of those pipelines.

limitations: All results are paper-reported; no independent execution or reproduction was performed.
The benchmark uses synthetic Sims 4 activity and deterministic symbolic rules; it does not establish inference about real people or actual household-agent performance.
Dialogue is generated using model-assisted pipelines and spot-checked; its validity as natural human evidence remains uncertain.

Vision-plus-language evaluation uses a two-stage video-to-diary then text-QA pipeline, while noiseless text-only input exposes structured evidence; performance differences therefore mix perception, summarization and reasoning.
Hint levels provide varying prior rule information; full-hint/noiseless conditions do not represent the ordinary deployed-agent setting.
Transfer to independently collected behavior, other simulators and real-world long-term interaction is unmeasured.

evidence_gaps.description: The benchmark results, generated episodes and input pipelines have not been independently audited or reproduced.
Transfer from deterministic synthetic household rules and generated dialogue to independently observed human behavior is unknown.

headline: LLM Inference in a Flash reports compressed KV caching and modeled Compute-in-Flash gains
dek: The paper combines integer-only compute-in-flash inference with a static flash-resident dictionary that stores compressed KV-cache codes. On LongBench, the authors report that the combined pipeline retains 99% of the FP16 full-KV baseline score across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B, with less than one average score-point degradation and nearly 15× dynamic KV traffic compression. Separately, an analytical model for Llama-3.1-8B at batch size 1 projects 3.1× lower decode latency and 2.7× lower energy at 1K context, and 4.4×/6.8× at 256K, against an NPU+DDR5 full-KV baseline. These system-level numbers are modeled, not measurements on physical Compute-in-Flash hardware; prefill is outside the study.
what_changed: The paper combines integer-only compute-in-flash inference with a static flash-resident dictionary that stores compressed KV-cache codes. On LongBench, the authors report that the combined pipeline retains 99% of the FP16 full-KV baseline score across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B, with less than one average score-point degradation and nearly 15× dynamic KV traffic compression. Separately, an analytical model for Llama-3.1-8B at batch size 1 projects 3.1× lower decode latency and 2.7× lower energy at 1K context, and 4.4×/6.8× at 256K, against an NPU+DDR5 full-KV baseline. These system-level numbers are modeled, not measurements on physical Compute-in-Flash hardware; prefill is outside the study.
why_it_matters: Long-context decoding can be limited by moving KV state between memory and compute. The paper reports a large reduction in dynamic KV traffic with small LongBench score changes, then models potential decode benefits on a Compute-in-Flash design. The modeled gains depend on assumptions about device bandwidth, dictionary placement and duplicate dictionary storage, and do not establish physical-device performance or prefill efficiency.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On LongBench, the authors report that their combined integer-only quantization and dictionary KV compression retains 99% of the FP16 full-KV baseline score for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B, with less than one average score-point degradation and nearly 15× dynamic KV-cache compression.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For Llama-3.1-8B at batch size 1, the paper's analytical system model projects 3.1× lower decode latency and 2.7× lower energy at 1K context, and 4.4× lower latency and 6.8× lower energy at 256K, for configuration S2 relative to an NPU+DDR5 full-KV baseline. These are modeled values, not physical-hardware measurements.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report near-FP16 LongBench scores with almost 15× dynamic KV-cache traffic compression for two model families, and analytically project lower decode latency and energy for one modeled Llama-3.1-8B configuration.
technical.compute_or_cost: The analytical model projects latency and energy reductions for one Llama-3.1-8B batch-size-1 decode configuration. It does not measure realized energy, device cost, throughput on a fabricated/available CIM-SSD device or end-to-end service economics.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports measured LongBench task scores and effective KV compression for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B. The reported system-level latency and energy savings are analytical model outputs for Llama-3.1-8B, not results measured on physical Compute-in-Flash hardware; the research desk did not reproduce either result.
technical.implementation_status: Research paper with LongBench evaluations and analytical system modeling; no physical Compute-in-Flash system result was verified.
technical.mechanism: Combines integer-only compute-in-flash operations with a flash-resident static dictionary. KV vectors are encoded as sparse codes over the dictionary; attention operates on codes while keeping a recent window in full precision. The design models SSD-CIM compute and memory movement for decode.
technical.novelty: Pairs sparse dictionary coding of the KV cache with integer-only compute tailored to compute-in-flash constraints, and evaluates both task score/traffic compression and modeled system-level decode costs.
technical.regime: LongBench combined-pipeline evaluation on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B. System model: Llama-3.1-8B, batch size 1, decode at 1K/64K/256K contexts, comparing NPU+DDR5 FP16 full-KV against modeled SSD-CIM INT8 variants. Prefill is not evaluated.
technical.reproducibility: Current arXiv v1 HTML and API metadata were inspected. No independent reproduction or physical-device execution was performed. System results depend on modeled bandwidth/compute assumptions and storing two copies of the value dictionary; prefill is explicitly left for future work.
technical.strongest_baseline: LongBench compares the combined method to FP16 with full KV cache. System model configuration S2 is compared to B1, an NPU+DDR5 DRAM FP16 baseline with full KV cache moved each decode step; B2 and S1 are additional modeled ablations.

limitations: LongBench and KV compression results are author-reported and were not independently reproduced.
Latency and energy improvements are analytical projections, not measurements on physical Compute-in-Flash hardware.
The system-level model covers decode only; mapping prefill efficiently is explicitly left as future work.
The model assumes two copies of the value dictionary, one transposed and one non-transposed, to support pursuit and attention.
System-level projections focus on Llama-3.1-8B, batch size 1 and modeled 1K/64K/256K context lengths; transfer to other models, hardware, concurrency and service loads is unknown.

evidence_gaps.description: LongBench accuracy and KV traffic compression have not been independently reproduced.
The projected latency/energy savings have not been validated on physical Compute-in-Flash hardware, and prefill is not modeled.

headline: A conditional-independence limit for confidence-ranked parallel diffusion sampling
dek: The authors analyze independent-update samplers that choose parallel token writes using per-position distributions and sample each selected position independently. They claim that matching the training joint distribution at a step requires the written positions to be conditionally independent given fixed tokens, and that per-position marginals alone cannot certify this condition. On their synthetic ScanAndAdd task, they report confidence-ranked writes with perfect sample-level validity metrics but a generated token distribution about 29 times the sampling-noise-floor total variation. The theorem is conditional on the sampler class; the measured distortion is from one synthetic task and is not evidence that deployed diffusion models exhibit the same magnitude of error.
what_changed: The authors analyze independent-update samplers that choose parallel token writes using per-position distributions and sample each selected position independently. They claim that matching the training joint distribution at a step requires the written positions to be conditionally independent given fixed tokens, and that per-position marginals alone cannot certify this condition. On their synthetic ScanAndAdd task, they report confidence-ranked writes with perfect sample-level validity metrics but a generated token distribution about 29 times the sampling-noise-floor total variation. The theorem is conditional on the sampler class; the measured distortion is from one synthetic task and is not evidence that deployed diffusion models exhibit the same magnitude of error.
why_it_matters: Parallel decoding can reduce generation steps, but good token-level confidence or sample validity does not by itself show that the joint output distribution matches the training distribution. The paper gives a precise condition for one class of independent-update samplers and a synthetic example where correctness and distributional fidelity diverge. This can inform sampler design and evaluation while leaving practical scale and transfer open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For an independent-update sampler whose parallel write set is selected using only per-position distributions (or randomness independent of the target joint distribution), the paper states that a product update matches the target one-step conditional only when the selected positions are conditionally independent given the fixed tokens. A dependent group cannot be represented exactly by that product.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the authors' synthetic ScanAndAdd task with a closed-form joint distribution, they report that confidence-ranked parallel writes yield perfect well-formedness, correctness and uniqueness metrics while the generated token distribution remains about 29 times the sampling-noise-floor total variation from the training distribution.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports that a hand-specified write order on ScanAndAdd can produce a token distribution not distinguishable from training samples at the measured sample size, while maintaining 0.987–0.996 correctness; this is an achievable task-specific ordering, not a general sampler rule.

technical.claimed_result: The authors claim a general per-step restriction for the defined sampler class and illustrate its effect on ScanAndAdd, where confidence-ranked multi-position writes select dependent groups. The paper says a domain-trained scheduler carrying information beyond current per-position distributions is outside Theorem 4's premise, although it must still avoid dependent product updates to match the joint distribution.
technical.compute_or_cost: No compute or economic cost comparison is established in the inspected claims. The paper reports a synthetic task and research-model training/decoding measurements, not deployment cost.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports closed-form checks and trained-model measurements on ScanAndAdd. The 29x sampling-noise-floor total-variation figure and perfect sample-level metrics are author-reported for this synthetic task; the research desk did not rerun the experiment or independently audit the proofs.
technical.implementation_status: Research paper and task-specific experiments only; no deployed system or independently reproduced implementation was verified.
technical.mechanism: Define an independent-update sampler as selecting a write set from per-position distributions and drawing each written token independently. The paper's core argument is that such a product can match a target joint conditional only where the selected coordinates are conditionally independent; marginal distributions do not identify all dependencies in the joint distribution.
technical.novelty: States a conditional-independence requirement and a marginal-information impossibility boundary for a defined class of per-position independent parallel updates, then connects sample correctness to a separate distribution-level metric on a synthetic task.
technical.regime: Independent-update samplers over masked discrete sequences, with write-set decisions based only on per-position distributions or independent randomness. Empirical illustration: one synthetic 25-position ScanAndAdd task with closed-form distribution and research models; not a product-model deployment evaluation.
technical.reproducibility: Current arXiv v2 HTML and API metadata were inspected. No code artifact or independent proof review was located or performed. The paper provides task/training details in Appendix A but results remain author-reported.
technical.strongest_baseline: On ScanAndAdd, confidence-ranked remasking is contrasted with hand-specified write orders designed around task structure. The latter are an achievable task-specific frontier, not a general decoding baseline; the paper also cites PUNT's approximate conditional-independence testing as related work.

limitations: The 29x total-variation result is measured on one synthetic task with a known closed-form distribution; the paper says its experiments do not duplicate product-model architectures, decoding strategies or deployments.

The theorem applies to the paper's defined independent-update sampler class. A scheduler with learned domain information beyond current per-position distributions is outside Theorem 4's assumption; the result is not a blanket impossibility for all parallel decoding.
Perfect sample-level well-formedness, correctness and uniqueness do not imply distributional match, but this gap was measured here only on ScanAndAdd.
The authors report mathematical results and experiments; the research desk did not independently audit the proof, run the code or reproduce the reported measurements.

The current paper cites PUNT, which already reports approximate conditional-independence testing for parallel sampling. The contribution should not be described as the first method to consider dependencies; the precise novelty boundary remains the paper's impossibility result under per-position-only information.
The arXiv HTML endpoint for PUNT returned 404; only its official abstract and API metadata were reviewed.

evidence_gaps.description: The ScanAndAdd experiment and theorem-to-implementation correspondence have not been independently reproduced or audited.
The distributional-fidelity effect outside ScanAndAdd, including natural text or image tasks and newer learned schedulers, is unknown.

headline: GraphEcho finds that repeated graph paths raise evidence-revisit rates, while provenance-aware training trades coverage for fewer repeats
dek: Wang et al. introduce GraphEcho, a controlled benchmark separating graph-path count from evidence-source count. In the paper’s reported tests, adding redundant supporting paths increased repeated evidence walks for all four frozen agents; a provenance-aware Qwen3-4B policy reduced revisits and raised accuracy on synthetic claims, but reached fewer distinct sources and scored lower on the SciFact transfer set. Static judgment effects varied by model.
what_changed: Wang et al. introduce GraphEcho, a controlled benchmark separating graph-path count from evidence-source count. In the paper’s reported tests, adding redundant supporting paths increased repeated evidence walks for all four frozen agents; a provenance-aware Qwen3-4B policy reduced revisits and raised accuracy on synthetic claims, but reached fewer distinct sources and scored lower on the SciFact transfer set. Static judgment effects varied by model.
why_it_matters: Graph retrieval agents can encounter one observation through several representations. The paper shows why evaluation should track evidence origins and unobserved sources alongside answer accuracy and repeated retrieval: a policy can become more efficient by stopping earlier while missing evidence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In GraphEcho’s controlled synthetic tests, redundant supporting paths raised repeated evidence-walk rates for all four frozen agents, while the effect on accuracy varied by model.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For the trained Qwen3-4B policy, the authors report a 41.47 percentage-point synthetic-accuracy increase over provenance metadata alone, accompanied by an 8.32-point decrease in source recall.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the paper’s SciFact transfer setup, PAPT reduced repeated walks but had lower accuracy than the frozen Qwen3-4B baseline; the three compared conditions each exposed only one document origin.

claims.label: INFERRED
claims.text: Reducing repeated retrieval does not by itself establish better evidence use, because a policy may stop earlier and leave distinct reachable sources unobserved.

technical.claimed_result: The authors conclude that efficient exploration and effective evidence use can diverge: policies that reduce repeated retrieval may stop before reaching distinct sources. Their synthetic benchmark and SciFact transfer results suggest that provenance-aware training can change this tradeoff, but its quality depends on domain and stopping behavior.
technical.compute_or_cost: Training uses Qwen3-4B with GRPO and LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32) for one epoch over 500 training examples, with one training seed. Full compute, inference and annotation costs are not reported in the inspected sections.
technical.demonstrated_result: The authors report that redundant supporting paths raise echo-walk rates for all four evaluated frozen agents by 5.80–38.84 percentage points across 200 synthetic claims and five presentation seeds. In a Qwen3-4B agentic setup, PAPT raises synthetic accuracy by 41.47 points versus provenance metadata alone while lowering source recall by 8.32 points; on 188 SciFact claims it lowers accuracy by 3.55 points while lowering echo rate by 36.00 points. These are paper-reported results, not independently reproduced findings.
technical.implementation_status: A research benchmark and training method described in arXiv v1. The inspected arXiv page exposes the paper and TeX/PDF links but no code repository link; implementation artifacts and independent reproduction were not located in this targeted check.
technical.mechanism: GraphEcho constructs graph paths that can refer either to the same evidence origin or to distinct origins, varying path multiplicity and source multiplicity separately. It measures model judgments and active exploration. Its provenance-aware post-training (PAPT) rewards verdict quality, source counting and distinct evidence acquisition while penalizing repeated acquisition and walk cost.
technical.novelty: Separates graph representation multiplicity from evidence-origin multiplicity and evaluates both conclusions and whether active exploration reaches distinct sources; evaluates acquisition metrics alongside answer quality.
technical.regime: One 800-claim synthetic benchmark (500 train, 100 development, 200 test) with controlled equal-weight evidence origins, plus SciFact development-set transfer. The agentic primary budget is six walk actions. Static judgments and active evidence acquisition are measured separately.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes datasets, controlled conditions, prompts/action environment and bootstrap procedures, but no public code was found in the inspected record. Training uses one random seed; no independent reproduction was found.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares four frozen agents with controlled redundant-path conditions, inference-time provenance and instruction controls, graph preprocessing that collapses equivalent paths, and PAPT. Its reported frozen-agent tests include Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B and GPT-5-mini; the principal trained policy is Qwen3-4B.

limitations: All empirical findings are reported by the preprint authors and have not been independently reproduced in this review.
Synthetic source independence and equal-strength evidence are controlled benchmark assumptions; real studies can share datasets, methods and biases.

The SciFact transfer experiment uses a one-document setting for the compared agent conditions and does not test multi-source acquisition; its static multi-document analysis includes only ten eligible claims.
PAPT training uses one random seed, so bootstrap intervals do not capture variation across separately trained policies.
The authors report model-dependent judgment responses; repeated-path exposure did not uniformly lower answer accuracy.
No public code or independent implementation was located in the inspected arXiv record.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported graph-agent and PAPT results have not been independently reproduced, and no public code artifact was located during this review.
SciFact transfer does not test multi-source active acquisition, and its static document-provenance analysis includes only ten eligible multi-document claims.

headline: UnifiedPlayers paper reports benchmark gains from jointly training planning, execution and executable evaluation policies
dek: The authors of arXiv:2609.20089 report UnifiedPlayers, a GRPO framework that alternately trains planning, tool-execution and executable-verifier policies using shared sandbox verdicts. On Qwen3-4B-Base and MiMo-7B-Base they report higher averages than their reimplementations of prior methods across seven math and five general reasoning/code benchmarks. what_changed: The authors of arXiv:2609.20089 report UnifiedPlayers, a GRPO framework that alternately trains planning, tool-execution and executable-verifier policies using shared sandbox verdicts. claims.label: CLAIMED

headline: SSD-LLaMA reports trillion-parameter MoE inference on a single RTX 5090
dek: The SSD-LLaMA preprint describes an SSD-to-RAM-to-VRAM expert-delivery system with a three-tier cache and CPU–GPU execution placement for MoE inference. On a stated consumer testbed with one RTX 5090, 16 GB host DRAM and a 4 TB NVMe SSD, the authors report running a 2.8T-parameter Kimi-K3 at 1.217 prefill tokens/s and 0.465 decode tokens/s. Section 5.4 reports baseline-specific throughput gains, while the abstract and conclusion give different aggregate ranges; the exact mapping is unresolved. These are paper-reported measurements, not an independent reproduction.
what_changed: The SSD-LLaMA preprint describes an SSD-to-RAM-to-VRAM expert-delivery system with a three-tier cache and CPU–GPU execution placement for MoE inference. Section 5.4 reports baseline-specific throughput gains, while the abstract and conclusion give different aggregate ranges; the exact mapping is unresolved. These are paper-reported measurements, not an independent reproduction.
why_it_matters: SSD-backed expert delivery may lower the hardware capacity needed to load large MoE models locally, which could change where inference is feasible. The reported Kimi-K3 decode rate is below one token per second, and the paper's speedup ranges conflict across sections, so it does not establish a general consumer-PC performance or cost frontier.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that SSD-LLaMA runs a 2.8T-parameter Kimi-K3 on a consumer testbed with one RTX 5090, 32 GB VRAM, 16 GB host DRAM and a 4 TB NVMe SSD, reaching 1.217 prefill tokens/s and 0.465 decode tokens/s.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For batch-size-1 tests across three evaluated MoE models, Section 5.4 reports prefill throughput gains of 1.90×–3.61× over llama.cpp and 1.06×–2.92× over KTransformers, and decode gains of 1.35×–3.44× over llama.cpp and 1.57×–15.61× over KTransformers; comparisons to Colibri are limited to GLM-5.2.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper's abstract and conclusion instead summarize prefill gains as 1.52×–4.19× and decode gains as 2.10×–15.58×. The source does not reconcile these aggregate ranges with the baseline-specific Section 5.4 values, so no single aggregate range is treated as settled here.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that SSD-LLaMA runs selected MoE models on a single consumer RTX 5090 and outperforms named CPU/GPU and SSD-offload baselines in batch-size-1 tests. The specific 2.8T Kimi-K3 result is 1.217 prefill tokens/s and 0.465 decode tokens/s; aggregate speedup ranges conflict between the abstract/conclusion and Section 5.4.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper models hardware capacity costs and reports an SSD/DRAM capacity-tier advantage, but no independently verified purchase-cost, energy, utilization or total-cost-of-service result was established in this review.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports the stated hardware setup, Kimi-K3 rates and baseline comparisons. the research desk inspected the paper's current v1 HTML and fetched the PDF but did not independently reproduce the measurements, inspect runnable code or verify the cited model checkpoints.
technical.implementation_status: Preprint-described prototype and author-reported testbed measurements; no independently runnable implementation or reproduction was verified.
technical.mechanism: Stores the full expert pool on NVMe and stages selected experts through host RAM into VRAM. The paper combines fixed-offset expert packs, asynchronous SSD reads and transfers, a three-tier cache, lossless block compression, and CPU/GPU placement selected using end-to-end token latency.
technical.novelty: A coordinated SSD–RAM–VRAM expert-delivery pipeline for sparse MoE inference that combines direct expert-pack reads, overlap, caching and CPU/GPU placement rather than treating SSD capacity as ordinary memory mapping.
technical.regime: Author-reported MoE inference on an Intel Ultra5 230F, RTX 5090 with 32 GB VRAM, 16 GB host DRAM and 4 TB NVMe SSD rated up to 9 GiB/s sequential read/write. Baseline tests use batch size 1 on MMLU and Alpaca; the paper evaluates DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi-K2.7-Code and GLM-5.2, and separately reports Kimi-K3 throughput.
technical.reproducibility: Current arXiv v1 HTML and API metadata were inspected and the PDF fetched. No independent run was performed. The paper's reported aggregate prefill/decode speedup ranges conflict with its Section 5.4 baseline-specific ranges; exact comparison scope remains unresolved.
technical.strongest_baseline: Section 5.4 compares against llama.cpp and KTransformers across the three stated model families, and Colibri only on GLM-5.2. The paper reports baseline-specific gains but its abstract/conclusion aggregate ranges do not reconcile with those section values.

limitations: All performance results are author-reported and were not independently reproduced; the paper's executable artifact and exact checkpoint revisions were not inspected.

The testbed is one configuration with batch size 1 and two prompt workloads; performance on other SSDs, CPUs, GPU memory configurations, concurrency levels and serving workloads is unknown.
The source's cost discussion is an estimate; this review did not verify hardware prices, energy, utilization, service cost or field deployment.
contradictory_evidence: Within this same paper, the abstract and conclusion report prefill 1.52×–4.19× and decode 2.10×–15.58×, while Section 5.4 reports different baseline-specific ranges (including 1.06×–3.61× prefill and 1.35×–15.61× decode across its named comparisons). evidence_gaps.description: The Kimi-K3 rates and baseline comparisons have not been independently reproduced, and implementation/checkpoint correspondence has not been audited.
The abstract/conclusion aggregate speedup ranges differ from the baseline-specific ranges in Section 5.4; the comparison set and aggregation are not reconciled.

headline: VA-Bench measures the gap between spatial diagnosis and successful robot action
dek: Zhang et al. introduce VA-Bench, a simulator benchmark requiring general-purpose multimodal models to use RGB-only demonstrations, actively choose camera views, issue metric Cartesian robot commands and revise actions from execution feedback. Across 14 base task families and 12 primary model conditions, the authors report three runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per task. The strongest tested condition has a three-run macro-average terminal task success of 53.93±3.17%, despite 100.0% target localization and 78.9% spatial-relation scores in its annotated run. In one matched active-camera versus passive five-view comparison, success rises from 27.86% to 57.50%; this comparison covers four model conditions and does not identify whether view relevance, cross-view integration or longer visual context explains the gain. No tested model completes the strict five-object long-horizon episode. These are author-reported benchmark results, not an independent reproduction.
what_changed: Zhang et al. introduce VA-Bench, a simulator benchmark requiring general-purpose multimodal models to use RGB-only demonstrations, actively choose camera views, issue metric Cartesian robot commands and revise actions from execution feedback. Across 14 base task families and 12 primary model conditions, the authors report three runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per task. The strongest tested condition has a three-run macro-average terminal task success of 53.93±3.17%, despite 100.0% target localization and 78.9% spatial-relation scores in its annotated run. In one matched active-camera versus passive five-view comparison, success rises from 27.86% to 57.50%; this comparison covers four model conditions and does not identify whether view relevance, cross-view integration or longer visual context explains the gain. No tested model completes the strict five-object long-horizon episode. These are author-reported benchmark results, not an independent reproduction.
why_it_matters: The benchmark separates describing or locating objects from acquiring useful visual evidence, grounding metric actions and completing manipulation. Its reported gap between strong intermediate diagnostics and terminal success, plus the bounded active/passive comparison, gives embodied-agent evaluation a way to test the full observe–reason–act–revise loop rather than perception alone. The simulator, finite task families and untested real-robot transfer limit generalization.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report a 14-family simulator benchmark with 12 primary model conditions and three runs over the same 20 verified seeds per base task; the strongest tested condition averaged 53.93±3.17% terminal success.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the strongest condition’s annotated run, the paper reports 100.0% target-localization and 78.9% spatial-relation scores, while no tested model completes the strict five-object long-horizon episode.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports one matched active-camera versus passive five-view comparison increasing success from 27.86% to 57.50%; the four-condition protocol comparison does not identify which aspect of active viewing causes the difference.

technical.claimed_result: In one matched comparison, active camera control raised task success from 27.86% to 57.50% relative to passive input containing five predefined views. The paper reports the comparison for four conditions; it does not isolate view relevance, cross-view integration or longer visual context as the cause.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports 14 base task families (11 single-arm, three dual-arm), seven held-out geometry/layout variants and one five-object long-horizon composition track. Twelve primary model conditions were evaluated in three runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per base task. The strongest reported condition averaged 53.93±3.17% terminal success; in its annotated run it scored 100.0% on target localization and 78.9% on spatial relations. No model completed a strict long-horizon episode. These are author-reported simulator results.
technical.implementation_status: The paper links a public benchmark and code repository. The repository was not audited or executed, and results were not independently rerun in this activation.
technical.mechanism: VA-Bench requires the model to learn task procedure from RGB-only demonstrations, choose camera viewpoints, estimate metric robot–object geometry, issue Cartesian targets through a fixed model-agnostic controller, then revise from execution outcomes. It withholds privileged object poses, oracle trajectories and learned action heads.
technical.novelty: Connects active visual evidence acquisition, demonstration-conditioned spatial re-grounding, metric action and feedback revision in a single evaluated loop, with terminal success and trajectory-level diagnostics.
technical.regime: A fixed simulated robot-manipulation suite with RGB observations, metric action commands and 20 verified seeds per base task. Primary terminal-success results use three runs per model condition; the trajectory diagnostics use one fully annotated run per condition. The long-horizon track composes five objects in one simulator task family.
technical.reproducibility: The paper provides task/protocol descriptions, seed counts, repeated-run summaries and linked code. Independent execution, simulator/annotation audit and new-task transfer remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: For active evidence acquisition, the paper compares camera control with passive observation that supplies five predefined views at each observation while preserving the same seeds, demonstrations, robot execution and terminal-success accounting. It also reports held-out geometry/layout transfer against the base-task regime.

limitations: All measurements are author-reported simulator results; no independent execution was performed.
The annotated behavioral diagnostics use one run per condition; terminal success is repeated across three runs.
The active/passive protocol comparison is limited to four model conditions and combines possible view relevance, cross-view integration and context-length effects.
Held-out geometry/layout variants are finite and do not establish arbitrary open-set or real-robot generalization.
The strict long-horizon result covers one five-object composition family.
The paper does not intervene on perception, planning and execution components to identify which causes each observed failure.

evidence_gaps.description: VA-Bench results and the active/passive comparison have not been independently executed.
The simulator task set and one five-object composition family do not establish open-set or real-robot transfer.

headline: A preprint reports that live tool-progress signals improved post-tool latency in one serving-engine experiment
dek: Liu et al. propose exposing execution progress from running agent tools to the serving system for KV-cache decisions. Their preprint reports a harness reading progress from tool output and environment state without changing the agent-visible result path, and an end-to-end experiment in a production engine. The authors report 20.7% lower p90 time to first token after tool calls with HBM only and 20.8% with HBM plus DRAM compared with LRU. These are paper-reported results, not an independent reproduction or evidence of general serving-system gains.
what_changed: Liu et al. propose exposing execution progress from running agent tools to the serving system for KV-cache decisions. Their preprint reports a harness reading progress from tool output and environment state without changing the agent-visible result path, and an end-to-end experiment in a production engine. The authors report 20.7% lower p90 time to first token after tool calls with HBM only and 20.8% with HBM plus DRAM compared with LRU. These are paper-reported results, not an independent reproduction or evidence of general serving-system gains.
why_it_matters: Tool execution can leave an agent request’s KV cache occupying scarce GPU memory while the agent waits. If the reported gains transfer, live tool progress could improve post-tool responsiveness and cache scheduling. Current evidence supports a specific paper-reported result, not a general performance guarantee.

technical.regime: One author-reported production-engine evaluation; workload mix and hardware need fuller audit; no broad serving-stack transfer established.

headline: VRR uses verification feedback to expand candidate search, with mixed reported benchmark results
dek: Tomihari and Ichikawa introduce Verify–Repair–Reselect (VRR), which feeds verifier diagnostics back into generation: after ranking an initial pool, it retains the winner, conditionally creates repairs of the winner and runner-up plus a new-approach candidate, filters invalid/duplicate outputs and reselects under the original criteria. Across two models and eight code/reasoning benchmarks, the authors report VRR beats fixed-pool LAV selection in 9 of 16 settings. Table 1 includes improvements as well as null and negative cells. On LiveCodeBench, the authors report recovery on some problems where all initial candidates were incorrect. These are paper-reported results using the same model for generation, verification and repair; matched total-inference-budget comparison with best-of-N and independent reproduction remain open.
what_changed: Tomihari and Ichikawa introduce Verify–Repair–Reselect (VRR), which feeds verifier diagnostics back into generation: after ranking an initial pool, it retains the winner, conditionally creates repairs of the winner and runner-up plus a new-approach candidate, filters invalid/duplicate outputs and reselects under the original criteria. Across two models and eight code/reasoning benchmarks, the authors report VRR beats fixed-pool LAV selection in 9 of 16 settings. Table 1 includes improvements as well as null and negative cells. On LiveCodeBench, the authors report recovery on some problems where all initial candidates were incorrect. These are paper-reported results using the same model for generation, verification and repair; matched total-inference-budget comparison with best-of-N and independent reproduction remain open.
why_it_matters: Verifier feedback can describe why candidates fail, not just which candidate ranks highest. Reusing that diagnostic information to generate alternatives could improve test-time search when every initial candidate is wrong. The paper’s mixed results, same-model verifier/generator and missing compute-normalized best-of-N comparison mean the gain should be treated as a bounded method result rather than general evidence that repair beats more sampling.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across two models and eight benchmarks, the authors report VRR improves over fixed-pool LAV selection in 9 of 16 settings; Table 1 also contains null and negative settings.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report VRR can recover correct LiveCodeBench solutions when every candidate in the initial pool is incorrect; the recovery result is not independently reproduced.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The same model performs generation, verification, repair and reselection; no matched total-inference-budget comparison against best-of-N was established in this review.

technical.claimed_result: The authors argue that verifier diagnostics can improve the candidate set and allow recovery beyond the initial pool. Whether gains persist against best-of-N under equal total generation-plus-verification compute is unresolved.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper evaluates Gemma 4 31B IT and Qwen3-32B across eight code and reasoning benchmarks, using identical frozen initial pools for Single, fixed-pool LAV and VRR. It reports that VRR improves over LAV in 9 of 16 model-benchmark settings. Table 1 includes negative results (for example -0.61 and -0.27 percentage points), null results (0.00) and positive cells (up to +4.04 points in the shown table). LiveCodeBench analysis reports some recovered correct answers even when every initial candidate was incorrect. These are author-reported results.
technical.implementation_status: The paper gives algorithm details, prompt templates and experimental settings. the research desk did not run the code or independently reproduce results.
technical.mechanism: VRR builds explicit evaluation criteria, verifies and ranks a frozen initial candidate set, and triggers repair when scores are low or judgments remain unresolved. It retains the initial winner, generates a local repair, a runner-up repair and a new-approach solution, screens malformed or duplicate candidates, then re-verifies and reselects under the original criteria.
technical.novelty: Uses criterion-level verifier feedback as a signal for expanding the candidate set, while retaining the original winner and applying the same criteria to final reselection.
technical.regime: Two models, eight code/reasoning benchmarks, five initial candidates for code and three for reasoning tasks. The same model performs generation, verification, repair and reselection. Verifier labels and private tests are withheld until answers are fixed; newly generated candidates are checked with public tests and format/duplicate filters.
technical.reproducibility: The paper provides prompt templates and benchmark configuration. Independent reproduction, compute-normalized comparisons, variance, and sensitivity to verifier/generator separation remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Fixed-pool LAV selection over the same frozen initial candidates, plus a Single first-candidate baseline. The paper does not establish a matched total-token/latency comparison with best-of-N independent sampling.

limitations: All results are paper-reported; the research desk did not execute code or independently reproduce the experiments.
VRR improves over fixed-pool LAV in 9 of 16 model-benchmark settings; the table includes null and negative cells.
The same model performs generation, verification, repair and reselection, so verifier errors may be inherited or amplified.
The paper does not establish that gains survive an equal total generation-plus-verification token or latency budget versus best-of-N sampling.

headline: SAFE paper measures whether four frontier models seek safety evidence before deployment decisions
dek: Omer Tafveez introduces SAFE, a two-stage benchmark in which models can inspect optional safety evidence before making deployment decisions and then respond to findings. The paper evaluates GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on 900 controlled environments with five rollouts per scenario. The authors report inspection responds more to severity and retrieval cost than to stated risk probability: raising probability from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points. A linked repository provides scenarios, saved outputs and analysis notebooks. This is a prompted, stylized benchmark, not a measure of latent motivation or autonomous open-ended evidence search; no independent rerun was found.
what_changed: Omer Tafveez introduces SAFE, a two-stage benchmark in which models can inspect optional safety evidence before making deployment decisions and then respond to findings. The paper evaluates GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on 900 controlled environments with five rollouts per scenario. The authors report inspection responds more to severity and retrieval cost than to stated risk probability: raising probability from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points. A linked repository provides scenarios, saved outputs and analysis notebooks. This is a prompted, stylized benchmark, not a measure of latent motivation or autonomous open-ended evidence search; no independent rerun was found.
why_it_matters: Safety evaluations often provide risk information up front. SAFE tests an earlier decision: whether a model chooses to gather optional evidence before acting, separately from what it does after seeing a finding. If validated in broader settings, this distinction could improve evaluation design. Current results are bounded to a controlled single-turn task and four models.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper introduces SAFE, a 900-environment, two-stage benchmark across five domains. It varies issue probability, severity, retrieval cost and evidence-channel presentation; models first choose whether to inspect and then choose a response if a finding is revealed.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 with five rollouts per scenario, the authors report inspection rises with issue severity and falls as numeric retrieval cost rises. Raising stated issue probability from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points in the reported main conditions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a targeted 50-scenario cost–obligation decomposition, adding a 60-point retrieval cost to the free/no-obligation baseline reduces inspection rates to 33% (GPT-5.5), 18% (o3), 72% (Opus 4.8) and 32% (Sonnet 4.6); the authors report explicit cancellation threats account for more of the obligation effect than remediation duty alone.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper links an author GitHub repository whose README describes code, scenarios, saved model outputs and analysis notebooks for SAFE. Repository availability does not independently validate the reported experiments.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report distinct acquisition policies across four models. Inspection varies more with severity and numeric retrieval cost than with stated issue probability; cost–obligation and counterfactual analyses suggest some explanatory variables models mention do not match variables that change choices in tested cases.
technical.compute_or_cost: Subject-model runs require paid API calls; provider/API costs are not summarized as a total economic cost in this review. The study’s numeric inspection costs are experimental point payoffs, not measured retrieval costs in deployed systems.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint and linked author repository demonstrate the benchmark design, reported analyses, and availability of saved experiment outputs/code. They do not independently establish the behavioral results or latent motivations.
technical.implementation_status: Author repository README lists scenario generation, experiment runners, saved model outputs, coded rationales and analysis notebooks. The notebooks can analyze saved data without provider calls; new subject-model runs require provider credentials and paid API access. This review inspected the README but did not execute the repository.
technical.mechanism: SAFE presents a two-stage prompted decision. The model may inspect optional evidence or skip and deploy; inspected cases then receive a finding and choose to halt, proceed or partially mitigate. A factorial scenario matrix varies probability, severity, retrieval cost and evidence channel; targeted cost–obligation and counterfactual edits test which variables change observed choices.
technical.novelty: The study makes optional evidence acquisition an explicit safety-evaluation target, distinct from response after a risk is already supplied. Its controlled benchmark is a research proposal, not a validated deployment measure.
technical.regime: 900 environments cross five domains with three issue probabilities, four severity levels, five cost conditions and three evidence channels. Four models are evaluated with five rollouts per scenario. Additional 50-scenario cost–obligation and selected counterfactual diagnostic subsets are analyzed separately.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links public code/data and the author README describes scenarios, saved outputs, and notebooks. This supports artifact availability, not independent reproduction; the current review did not run the notebooks or provider-dependent experiments.
technical.strongest_baseline: No competing benchmark baseline is central to the paper; its main comparison is within-model behavior across controlled scenario conditions. The article compares channel formats and counterfactual variants rather than external evaluation methods.

limitations: The study measures prompted observable choices and generated explanations, not latent motivation. Absence of a strategic-ignorance rationale does not rule out internal information avoidance.

The 900 scenarios are a stylized single-turn benchmark. Models are explicitly offered an inspection action with stated costs, probabilities and payoffs; autonomous open-ended evidence search is not tested.
The study evaluates four models from two providers; results may differ under less evaluation-like deployment conditions.
The high-severity condition combines increased harm with protected-group bias and legal exposure, so it is not a pure severity scalar.
Evidence Discovery changes wording because it has no named report, so the channel contrast is not a minimal presentation-only intervention.
Counterfactual cases are selected for diagnostic sensitivity; their flip rates do not estimate population-wide treatment effects.

Rationale-monitor labels are imperfect: Stage 2 agreement is 81.1% with one annotator and 67.8% with another on a stratified sample; labels are approximate and not direct evidence of causal reasoning.
The author repository exposes saved outputs and analysis materials, but no independent rerun or external validity study was performed here.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the model inspection patterns or controlled interventions was located. Author-reported saved outputs and code do not establish independent validation.
SAFE uses a prompted single-turn setting that explicitly offers evidence gathering with numeric payoffs. It does not test autonomous recognition of missing information or open-ended search.

The high-severity manipulation changes harm type by adding systematic demographic bias and legal exposure; severity is not a pure scalar. Evidence Discovery also requires different wording, limiting attribution to channel framing alone.

Rationale labels use an ordered monitor ontology; Stage 2 monitor agreement is below one human annotator and selected counterfactual cases are diagnostic, not population estimates. Rationale text does not directly establish latent motivation.
